Galves Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division I just wondered -- so I wanted to, in terms of the ramp -- and congratulations on launching the vehicle on time and the great reviews it's been getting. As to the -- I mean, first of all, it's worth noting that it is actually normal in the auto industry for there to be an exponential growth in production so this not unusual. I was merely going over a slightly longer period of time than is normally the case for gasoline cars, because in our case, we've got something like 97% to 98% of the components of the Model S are new than any other vehicle, and you can only make cars as fast as your slowest component. And we want to make very sure that every car that comes off the line is as close to perfect as possible. In fact, I'm personally inspecting the cars whenever I can. I think it makes sense to take that approach and ensure that when customers receive a car, it is as close to flawless as possible, and only growth of the production ramp to the degree we're able to maintain an exceptional quality standard rather than to sort of rush into things and then have greater customer happiness. And when we look at cash flow forecasts, whether we did a bunch more deliveries in the third quarter or if basically it moves sort of several hundred deliveries from third to fourth quarter, one way or the other, it doesn't change our cash flow point. And we really need to be optimizing for our cash flow point-- from a cash flow standpoint. And then on the other side, making sure that our customers are ecstatic when they get their cars. And so I actually changed the production ramp to slow it down at the beginning and then ramp it up faster towards the end. And I think it's the right decision.
